newsitem.title: USA: Consumer spending, incomes up modestly in May.
newsitem.headline: Consumer spending, incomes up modestly in May.

text.p: Consumer spending picked up modestly in May from April's pace as incomes kept growing, the Commerce Department said on Monday, suggesting steady economic expansion ahead.

Spending increased 0.3 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $5.37 trillion after a slight 0.1 percent gain in April. Incomes from wages, salaries and all other sources rose an identical 0.3 percent in May to $6.77 trillion following a 0.2 percent pickup in April.

May incomes benefited from the economy's momentum after six years of unbroken expansion as private-sector wages and salaries climbed at a $9.5 billion annual rate compared with a much smller $2.7 billion gain in April.
Spending on costly durable goods like new cars and furniture partly recovered from an April slump, rising 0.2 percent to a rate of $644.9 billion after a 1.7 percent drop in April.

Consumers spent 0.1 percent less in May on nondurable goods like food and paper products as the spending rate fell to $1.58 trillion. But they boosted spending on services from April by 0.5 percent to $3.14 trillion.

The economy's steady growth has apparently bolstered consumer confidence and willingness to spend. With prices remaining well in check, policy-setting members of the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee are widely expected to keep interest rates steady when they meet to consider strategy on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The Labour Department is scheduled to release employment figures for June on Thursday amid expectations another 222,000 jobs were generated by the growing economy.

Gains in personal income, which includes wages and salaries as well as income from sources such as dividends, interest and businesses, are essential for funding consumer purchases, which fuel two-thirds of national economic activity.
Personal savings in May were at an annual rate of $297.5 billion, down slightly from $298.4 billion in April.
But the savings rate, a figure widely watched by economists that shows savings as a percentage of disposable income, was unchanged from April at 5.1 cents out of every dollar of income.
Payrolls of manufacturing companies grew slightly in May to an annual rate of $700 billion from $699.5 billion in April.
